newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German econ gloom seen keeping Bunds happy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German econ gloom seen keeping Bunds happy.

text.p: While German jobless lines grow ever longer and an embattled Bonn government implores Germans to tighten their belts for years to come, investors in the domestic bond market have little to complain about.
They are riding a rally that has seen yields on 10-year government bonds fall to about 5.6 percent now from about 6.6 percent last June, and which shows no signs of a big reversal.

Ten-year yields are likely to test their all-time low of 5.48 percent in the first quarter of 1997 and Bund futures, which on Wednesday reached an all-time high of 103.18, should hit 103.75, analysts say.
Bund futures slid below 103 later in the day in what dealers described as a consolidation. They fell as low as 102.75, down 20 basis points from Tuesday's close.
The upturn is fed by economic gloom pervading Germany which ensures there is virtually no chance of an interest rate rise in the foreseeable future.

Some analysts even believe the Bundesbank will never again raise rates before it cedes control of monetary policy to the European Central Bank in January 1999 at the scheduled start of the single currency.

A rate rise is regarded as out of the question given last week's data showing German unemployment surged by more than half a million people in January to a new post-war record of 4.66 million, a level last seen in the 1930s.

The news sparked criticism of Bonn's handling of the jobs crisis and Chancellor Helmut Kohl was condemned by trade unions on Wednesday for saying Germans should accept little or no wage increases over the next few years to help create jobs.

While chartwatchers warn that Bunds have risen so sharply that the market looks overbought at current levels, many traders do not expect an imminent sell-off and regard consolidation followed by further gains as much more likely.
They say any price falls are likely to be seized as buying opportunities by investors queuing up to put their cash in German bonds.
"German fundamental data give no reason why the rally should be over," said Werner Kraemer, bond analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Frankfurt.
"There are strong capital inflows, the insurers, the funds, all the domestic investors are swimming in money and don't know what to do with it."

But Kraemer adds that German yields are likely to rise in the next three months because of possible losses in the U.S. Treasury market should upcoming data strengthen the case for an interest rare increase.
Christoph Anhamm, bond analyst at UBS in Frankfurt, sees Bund futures starting a downward correction in the coming days which could take the market down two to two-and-a-half points.

"But from that level, if there has been no significant change in the fundamentals and in the U.S. market, we have wonderful potential to return to exactly where we are now and perhaps go even higher."

Even though German yields are close to record lows, investors now see Bunds as a safer bet than recent strong performers like high-yielding Italian and Spanish bonds which have little potential for further gains, analysts say.

Investors are also being lured into Bunds by the mark's recent weakness against the dollar. The U.S. currency on Wednesday surged to about 1.69 marks early on Wednesday and was trading at 1.6860 marks by 1230 GMT.
Longer maturities are the main beneficiaries given the current steepness of the German yield curve, analysts say.

"As long as it (the economy) remains weak and the signs for a recovery are weak then the trend is to go into long maturities given the steep yield curve," said Peter Kerger, portfolio manager at Credit Suisse Capital Management.
